Uniform Title: *Candrajñānāgama* Manuscript: BHU C4243 Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: April 7, 2012 Country of Publication: India śrī gurave śivāye namaḥ |
Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Self.
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas; homage!
Oṃ, homage to Viṣṇu.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva, to him who is auspicious, to the giver of auspiciousness; homage, homage!
Now, the Candrajñāna is being written.
Oṃ! [I bow to] Maheśvara, the God of gods, who dwells in the center of the Kailāsa throne, surrounded by Skanda, Nandin, and the Gaṇas, and accompanied by Viśveśvara. || 1 ||
It stood together with Brahmā and the other causal deities, accompanied by Umā,
joined by Mahodara, and surrounded by Apsarases.

The god was established in the great meditative absorption (mahādhyāna), surrounded by sages, accompanied by hosts of gandharvas and others, and joined by throngs of perfected beings (siddhas). || 3 ||
It was being heard by the best of gods, by the Sādhyas, Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts,
as well as by Nārada and others who were experts in song and dance.
The Lord of Gods, the bestower of boons, the cause of the world, the performer of universal grace, and the destroyer of all sins, was being propitiated. || 5 ||
There [he saw] Śiva, the Lord of the gods, accompanied by Umā, who is the supreme lord of all mantras, saluted by all the deities, and established therein. (6)
But having seen that boon-granting god, the skull-bearer absorbed in meditation,
Candra, the lord of those who know the Vedas, became possessed of a mind filled with doubt.
Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord with the eight-limbed salutation,
he spoke these words while weeping and sighing again and again.
Indeed, I behold this Indra’s net—an unreality that has attained the appearance of reality;
the entire cosmic egg, including all things mobile and immobile, is deluded by Māyā.
It is my conviction that the certain understanding of all—gods, humans, animals, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas—has utterly perished. 10.
But for form and likewise for sound, O Lord, which are momentary as you have stated, there is nevertheless a constant cognition of the form of the moon. (11)
O Lord, how can those subject to destruction pay homage to space? For it is like one who, having himself perished, imagines through thought that he has not been destroyed. (12)
How could sound possess both the quality of being produced and the status of a mantra?
It is just like a lute that has been played, endowed with the resonance of its strings. (13)
By the mind is led that for whom there are the six notes, the middle note, and the deity;
likewise, the mantras and thousands of vidyās take on that same form. (14)
Those of unawakened intellect are deluded; they perceive their own mind as existing externally.
Deceived by illusion once again, they find no satisfaction in that which is merely contrived.
O Lord, how can that which is unreal, like a magician’s trick, have such a form?
Those mantras being recited by you have not been correctly uttered by you. (16)
Deluded by false knowledge and arrogant, the gods and gandharvas are all like illusions and dreams; so too are the mudrās, meditations, and dhāraṇīs. (17)
That web of scriptures consisting of ritual manuals is not at all false or insignificant;
for it belongs to the Goddess, Vināyaka, Ṣaṇmukha, and Trilocana. (18)
Likewise, [the hymns] of Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Kaubera, and Uśanas;
as well as those of Vāsuki and Gāruḍa, and of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. (19)
It is that which was compiled by the sages headed by Sanatkumāra, whose souls were purified,
as well as by the munis headed by Durvāsas and others.
And there are mantras of various forms, as well as thousands of goddesses;
there are also various types of sciences (vidyās) obtained in their thousands. || 21 ||
And they were recounted as before, concisely and with logical reasoning;
that I heard, O Great God, while you were pleased and situated upon my head.
All those great lords were led astray by me through my exertion; the knowledge concerning the body, which is hidden from view, was not understood by any of them. (13)
And because their intellects are unawakened, they wander through the thicket of scriptures;
not satisfied with anything artificial, they remain ensnared by their own minds.

In one tantra after another, you have composed [works] that follow the path of scriptures never heard by me; you have not spoken with respect toward anyone, and thus those seeking the ultimate truth have been deluded. (15)
What is the so-called "created" mantra, and whose is the intellect that performs action?
To whom is the funeral cake (piṇḍa) given, and into what does the wind dissolve within the wind? (16)
The waters dissolve into the waters; fire enters into fire;
likewise, space into space, as do the mind, the intellect, and the ego.
Just as they had gone, they returned and merged back into their respective places;
for what is this fleshy body—whether burnt or devoured by living beings? (18)
The living soul (jīva) is indeed formless, devoid of qualities, beginningless, and indivisible;
it has neither form nor color, nor location, nor any mental concentration (dhāraṇā). (19)
Whose is time? Whose is fame? And whose are the most terrible soldiers? What are the hells? What are the edicts? And who is he in whom the merit of the deceased shall dwell? (20)
Those men who have been slain in battle by the thousands are led away over a long period of time; would one lead them, or rather, many? (21)
The birds became distressed and perished upon its emergence;
many numbering in the hundreds of thousands were destroyed there—has the Time of Destruction arrived? || 22 ||
Indeed, at one and the same time, thousands and even billions of beings are led away by many [messengers]; tell me, what is the reason for all this? (23)
Listen, O Candra, I shall proclaim a secret difficult to find on earth;
it has not been told to anyone, and it is the supreme means for removing all doubt. 24.
A mantra is not something to be adopted based on the combination of phonemes or other such factors, for it is intent upon action;
rather, O Supreme Lord, the Mātṛkā is joined with those [phonemes] for the purpose of delusion. (25)
Just as the vowels and consonants arise upon the path of their own self-knowledge through the gross path of the phonemes, so do they exist for all beings. || 26 ||
That which exists between the imperishable and the perishable—the imperishable that transcends even the imperishable—its substratum cannot be described by words. (27)
Deluded by false pride, they do not know that syllable;
yet, having known that king of seeds situated between Varuṇa and Anala— || 28 ||
One shall not be born again in a womb, even if one were a slayer of a Brahmin;
[the state] is devoid of name and caste, with the expansion of limbs and retinue.
The Ekavīra mantra is taught as a concise ritual procedure for accomplishment;
having abandoned the state of sound, it abides in the form of pure awareness.
The first sound is to be known as sound; that sound is devoid of sound.
This soundless, supreme mantra is the certain bestower of liberation upon yogins. (31)
Tuṭis, nine nimeṣas, as well as kāṣṭhās, kalās, and the Śaśadhara-vidyā, along with muhūrtas, days, and nights; || 32 ||
A fortnight, a month, the two solstices, and a year are known as "darkness" (tamas);
thus, O King of the Twice-born, time is designated by means of this piercing (kīlana).
Indeed, time, which is the very form of action, having become latent within the performed deed,
carries one away while residing in the body by means of that action which takes the form of time.
In the ultimate sense, there is neither creation nor transformation for Time;
the living being experiences the fruit of its own karma alone. (35)
The one Destroyer, Kṛtānta, seizes the hearts of living beings in an instant;
those creatures whose lifespan has expired—be they animals, humans, or gods—are all taken by him. (36)
For the sake of regulating them, time proceeds; it does not proceed out of hatred nor out of dispassion. Time performs this action—so it is said. (37)
Who is this that is led by Time? What is its form, O Śaṅkara? What is its nature, O Lord of the gods, O Great Lord of all living beings? (38)
In what place does the living being dwell, and from where does it die? O Three-eyed One, how does Time bring about its cessation within the abode of the living being? (39)
O Lord, tell me all this in brief according to its true nature;
first listen, for I shall proclaim a secret that is difficult to find on earth. (40)
For how can the soul—which is beginningless, stainless, partless, and free from passion—be eternally situated within the womb of power (śakti), its form devoid of meditation? (41)
Devoid of means of valid cognition and logic, you are the causeless and stainless one;
O Moon, listen, the vessel is conceived by the power of analogy. (42)
The Vaidika [power] is said to be a hundredth part of the tip of a hair;
it is to be known as threefold, and is traditionally remembered as Śākta, Grāhya, and Kāraka.
It is peaceful, empty, without appearance, immeasurable, and stainless;
it is devoid of all analogies and free from conceptual construction and time. || 44 ||

The second [category] is that whose form is whatever power (śakti) it may be; however, Prakṛti, which consists of the qualities (guṇas), should be understood as having the nature of the principles (tattvas). 45.
The five great elements, along with mind, intellect, and ego—this is the evolved primordial nature (prakṛti) that resides within all embodied beings. 46.

Having heard all the details of her ritual procedure, characterized by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) and so forth, Candra, the foremost among those who know the Vedas, laughed with derision.
Having laughed for a very long time, the king of the twice-born spoke this:
"O Lord, this body consists of the five elements and has gone to the five locations. (48)
In its own place, the mind, intellect, and ego dissolve;
whatever states have arisen in whatever manner, they likewise go to dissolution therein. (49)
O Omniscient One, tell me the definitive resolution of this doubt.
Listen to this declaration of the true nature, a secret born of nectar, [revealed] by Brahmā and the others in embodied form, as well as by the King of the Vedas and Yama. (51)
Likewise, by Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, Vitta-pa, and Vāyu, this unsurpassed scripture concerning the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) was composed for their own sake. || 52 ||
The rice-ball offering (piṇḍa), the monthly ancestral rite (māsika-śrāddha),
and likewise the annual rite (sāṃvatsarika) are for the sake of progeny and serve as the means of sustenance for all living beings.
The treatise has been composed for the sake of the people; they bestow food upon one another.
This world of living beings, the source of all existence, subsists by means of food. (54)
But because the soul is essentially formless and immutable, rites such as the offering of funeral cakes and the pouring of water do not apply to it. (55)
For one who is devoid of all analogies and free from conceptual construction, whence can there be a funeral body, whence a śrāddha rite, and whence the characteristics of cremation and so forth? (56)
O best of the twice-born, the Śrāddha rite honored by Brahmā and others is for the purpose of delusion; it has been refined by you as a cause for the maintenance of the world and its beings.
O best of the lords of the twice-born, the name "action" (karman) applies to all things;
one experiences happiness through one's own action and experiences suffering through one's own action. (58)
And just as one performs an action, so indeed does one experience its result again;
by whatever nature one abandons the body situated in Prakṛti.
By that very path, they each experience their own karma;
the individual soul transmigrates through bodies and does not die again. (60)
For the sake of birth one abandons the body, and for the sake of action one abandons the very body;
yet it is neither destroyed nor born, neither bound nor liberated.
Just as he is born again while remaining within the power [of Māyā], so too the creative action of all embodied beings is enveloped by the bonds of the guṇas. 62.
Its action remains present as a shadow according to its arrangement;
by whatever disposition one goes forth from within, one returns again to primordial nature (prakṛti).
By that indeed, the primordial karma proceeds in various places;
the living soul, liberated from the pairs of opposites, remains well-established in all actions.
O Lord of the twice-born, there is nothing in the three worlds that exists devoid of him, just as there is no wind within the enclosure of one who is standing still. 65.
Likewise, in all beings there is indeed a power in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa);
that which resides therein as the supreme void is known as the lunar life-force (candra-jīva). || 66 ||
O lord of the twice-born, how could that which is the void, the bearer of reality, ever perish, even through the dissolution of the conjunction of time? (67)
Just as wind situated in the sky appears within a jar, yet when the jar is suddenly broken, that wind is no longer found anywhere; so it is with the self. 68.
Thus, though residing within the entire body, it does not burn upon the fall of the body,
just as the reflection of the sun in water does not burn when joined with the face reflected in a mirror.
When the mirror is broken, O Moon, the reflection is lost, but the moon itself is not destroyed;
just as the sun never perishes at all due to the depletion of its water.
Thus, upon the destruction of the body, the embodied soul is neither destroyed nor bound;
it is all-pervading, the creator of all, and transcendent beyond all dualities.
For him there is no reckoning of time, nor indeed passion or hatred;
from flowers comes fragrance, from sesame seeds oil, from milk clarified butter, and from that, Nala.
Just as it exists within the fuel, so does that supreme, all-pervading one;
the individual soul (jīva), situated within the power (śakti), is not defiled at all. 73.
Just as the sky, though omnipresent, remains within the interior of a house, yet when that house is destroyed by fire, that sky is not destroyed at all. (74)
Thus, abiding within the entire body, he is indeed of the nature of emptiness and untainted;
for him there is neither time nor death, nor is there a physical body characterized by funeral rites.
This declaration of its true nature has now been revealed by me;
having heard this today, Candra, whose eyes are like blossoming lotuses, [was moved]. (76)
"O Lord, today I have heard from you something unprecedented and wonderful.
What is the nature of Prakṛti, and what is her form? O Bhairava, tell me her measure, her instrument, and her proof. (78)
Translucent, without head or feet, slightly hunched, and having the form of a thread, she moves and enters again by means of the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths. (79)
All qualities reside within her, who is as crooked in form as a serpent and whose body is the size of a hair-tip, just as impurities reside in a gem.
The supreme power, whose nature is like a jewel, possesses qualities comparable to coloration;
by this or that inherent nature, it abides in this or that [manifestation]. (81)
In the fourteenfold creation, there is a supreme power called Śakti;
it is like a reflection in a mirror or stars in the midst of water.
Likewise, the qualities born of primordial nature (prakṛti) are seen residing within the power; however, embodied beings experience them through their own actions and inherent disposition.
The individual soul (jīva) resides within the womb of power (śakti), like a sound residing within a bamboo flute;
thus, the soul devoid of power is said to be one that bestows neither happiness nor joy.
From the feet up to the crown of the head, it is established everywhere;
whatever form is seen, from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) up to Śiva, [is that very same reality]. (85)
And there within that interior, the Lord himself is situated as a void;
he exists both within the stone and as the hollow of the bone. || 86 ||
Devoid of that, the vital breath (prāṇa) does not perform its coming and going.
Today I shall tell you this secret; listen with one-pointed attention and devotion. 87.
Beyond this are all the directions, earth, water, fire,
as well as wind, ether, mind, intellect, ego, and those which are the qualities (guṇas).
All is empty and without support; therein all things are established.
Whatever exists as any kind of entity is situated within form. 89.
Therefore, that form of the moon is utterly insubstantial and remains like a dream;
abandon this delusion, O son, for everything is established in the void.

From the Void (śūnya) proceeds Power (śakti); from Power, the phonemes (varṇa) were born; from the phonemes likewise arise the mantras, and from the mantras comes the imperishable creation (sṛṣṭi). 91.

Therefore, one should meditate on the world as empty, so that it may never perish; for from that [emptiness] comes the beginning of the ages, and today, and always, that which is beyond existence is eternally existent.
Residing in the heart, it is not perceived at all; for it is all-seeing and untainted.
It has no physical body, nor does it require ancestral rites, nor is there any reckoning of time for it.
Devoid of all activity, he remains and is not at all defiled;
as the Lord, he dwells within the power of all the multitudes of beings. (94)
By that [Brahman], everything—both external and internal—is established;
it alone remains as the supreme excellence of all, residing within the vessel.
A distinction of rituals, actions, and qualities exists among the mantras;
however, no distinction in knowledge is found among them in the scriptures and traditional teachings.

"Even now, O Lord of Gods, I have not understood the nature of this magical illusion (indrajāla), nor its primordial cause (prakṛti), just as one does not understand the earth that supports all foundations. (97)
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, you have previously well-concealed the individual soul (jīva) within the scripture; it has not perished, nor is there any confusion even now.
O Lord of Gods, speak of its true nature so that I may understand it once again.
Just as dewdrops fallen from the moon into the sky are like that, having fallen into the middle of a lake, they dissolve and become one. (100)
Likewise, Śakti is the abode of the gods of the qualities (guṇas) and the bearer of their attributes;
she whose quality is the state of being without qualities, and whose form is indeed formless. 101.
Whatever exists of such a kind, established within the womb of Śakti,
by that all this is pervaded, up to the very end of the world of Brahmā.

From that, ritual actions proceed; this world is said to have its cause therein, consisting of the individual (āṇava), the empowered (śākta), and that which is of the nature of the point (bindu) and the resonance (nāda). 103.
And the movement of the vital airs, consisting of the moments of prāṇa and apāna, is entirely composed of Śiva; O Moon, Śiva is proclaimed to be the individual soul (jīva). || 104 ||
Having abandoned the web of scriptures and the subsequent web of logic, one who practices the awakening of spiritual knowledge, which contains the power within, [attains the goal]. || 105 ||
O Moon, he does not perish at all, nor is there any end to his time;
he truly becomes one who is free from old age and death—of this there is no doubt. || 106 ||
The individual soul (jīva) is neither born nor dead; it remains as that which moves between the higher and the lower.
It is likewise produced from the great elements and the qualities (guṇas) of actions.
But Prakṛti is the supreme Śakti, wherein the characteristic of delusion resides; I shall tell you this entire, most secret mystery. (108)
As long as the supreme reality remains unperceived, one must not abandon the sequence of ritual actions;
for embodied beings there are two states: that of the bound soul (paśu) and that of the Lord (pati). (109)
Indeed, due to its state as a bound soul (paśu), that which arises from the nectar is seized by the web of karma, just as the sun's rays are obscured by clouds and a mirror by dirt. 110.
Just as a crystal is covered by dust, so too is knowledge veiled by darkness;
due to ignorance, a living being is seen bound by the fetters of the guṇas.
One experiences the enjoyment of karma while remaining within one's own wombs;
indeed, the body does not die, for it continues to consume the enjoyment of karma.
But the awakened one, the omniscient Supreme Lord, attains knowledge through practice;
through knowledge he is liberated, and as one who is liberated, he is the liberator.
Whether one be an outcaste, of low birth, a dog-eater, or even a *phukkasa*, [one may realize] the Supreme God who pervades all and is free from causes and limiting conditions. (114)
He who knows [this] correctly regarding the moon is considered the supreme yogi;
whether he be a brahmin or one of dull intellect, he is indeed untouched by ignorance. (115)
Whether he be a Caṇḍāla or a man of knowledge, a gift should be given to him;
indeed, one should accept it from his hand, for he is to be honored just like me.
Abandon delusion indeed, O Candra, for this is the knowledge you have attained;
from ignorance comes the realm of ritual action, but from knowledge comes the destruction of karma. || 117 ||
There is neither fixed rule nor time; abandon this delusion.
Through ignorance, one is bound again by the bonds of karma and by primordial nature (prakṛti). 118.
O Moon, for those who are awakened, the entire world is always composed of omniscience;
the whole world, or even one's own body, is filled with supreme bliss. (119)
Having abandoned all doubts, he should indeed become one with the ground of emptiness;
there is no Time, nor Yama, for these are merely terrors for the childish. 120.
No comparison applies to that which is devoid of conceptual construction;
for one who is thus [devoid], whence can there be time, whence death, or how could there be teachings regarding hell? (121)
One should meditate on everything as consisting of emptiness, including every limb and member of the body;
having rendered the body empty, one should not conceptualize anything at all.
Living beings sink into the womb of conceptual construction; moreover, the deluded ones, devoted to evil, are bound again by the snares of the qualities of nature. 123.
For wherever they are born within another womb by their own karma, there, in that very state, the condition of being ignorant beings— like cattle— shall be ever-present.
O God, tell me this in truth: to whom indeed do actions belong?
For if the individual soul (jīva) is liberated, formless, and of the nature of space; || 125 ||
O Lord, bearer of the skull, how can there be action for that which is formless and indeed void? This I wish to hear from you out of your grace. (126)
What action can Prakṛti perform for that which is empty and doubled [the Puruṣa]?
Prakṛti, though full of qualities, likewise dies and is born. (127)
Just as one experiences the actions performed by oneself, so too does one experience them again;
neither the individual soul (jīva) experiences the action, nor does primordial nature (prakṛti) with its qualities (guṇas).
He is neither bound nor liberated; he is non-abiding and devoid of a fixed location.
He is omniscient, the overseer of all, whose nature is space, whose mind is space, and who moves through space.
Thus have I seen the yogis—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Bhārgava;
even they have fallen into perpetual delusion regarding the knowledge of the living soul (jīva). 130.
And I shall speak the truth; O foremost of the twice-born kings, listen! For the sake of the activity of beings, I remain established in the nature of things as they truly are.
In that same way, the entire world is bound together like clusters of gems in a stream of urine; I am that embodied Śakti, the foundational Earth who bears all. (132)
Situated in the midst of that, the individual soul (jīva) is the pervasive Lord whose nature is space;
it remains all-pervading, just as the sky situated within a house remains omnipresent. 133.
Just as that living soul is lost when the house collapses and the support falls,
so too is Brahman all-pervading and perfectly established everywhere.
O Lord of the Stars, abandon your delusion; what more shall I say to you? (35)
O Lord, this most profound secret, difficult to find on earth, the supreme characteristic of living beings, has been understood by me through your grace. (36)
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic penance has become fruitful.
Today I have truly been born, O God Bhairava, through this knowledge.
The Great God Maheśvara, the God of gods, was indeed gratified by this great king of hymns, just as he had been propitiated by Candra.
Having been thoroughly satisfied, the God granted a boon according to the prescribed rite:
"By my word, Jñānabhogin shall arise from the previously mentioned nectar. (39)
"O highly fortunate one, she shall become mine; this is my firm resolve.
When the god Maheśvara had spoken thus and ceased, [the goddess spoke].
And Candra attained knowledge; therefore it is known as Candra-jñāna.
This should be bestowed upon a devoted, wise person who is capable of receiving it with faith. 41.
He who disregards this scripture out of delusion is a fool; he should always remain endowed with self-knowledge. 42.
